slides.misconceptions: Pupils may treat the figures as fixed limits rather than typical estimates. Clarify that STM is often given as about 7 ± 2 items and 18–30 seconds without rehearsal; capacity and duration can vary with the task. “Modality-specific” means sensory memory briefly preserves the form of incoming information, such as sounds or visual features.
slides.background: These properties are associated with the stores in Atkinson and Shiffrin’s model. Coding describes the form in which information is represented, not how accurate or meaningful it is.
slides.run: Spend about 5 minutes checking what coding, capacity and duration mean. Ask pupils to compare the three stores and explain one difference to a partner.

slides.misconceptions: Pupils may think attention moves information straight into LTM, or that rehearsal guarantees LTM storage. In the model, attention transfers selected sensory information to STM; rehearsal keeps it active and may support transfer to LTM. Retrieval brings stored information from LTM into STM.
slides.background: Control processes are mental operations that regulate how information is handled. The model distinguishes these processes from the three stores themselves.
slides.run: Spend about 6 minutes tracing the route through the stores together. Ask pupils to name the process at each transition, then have them explain the route to a partner.

slides.misconceptions: Pupils may say the code is stored in LTM simply because Amir repeats it, or that recall means the code returns directly to awareness from LTM. Explain that rehearsal supports transfer to LTM, and retrieval brings information from LTM into STM for conscious use.
slides.background: Repeating the code aloud is an example of maintenance rehearsal. The model proposes that prolonged rehearsal supports transfer, but this does not mean every rehearsed item is stored permanently.
slides.run: Spend about 5 minutes following Amir’s example through the diagram. Ask pupils to identify the store and process at each stage, then recap the route as a class.

answers: Attention selects the locker code from the sensory register and transfers it to STM.
STM is mainly acoustic. Repeating the code is maintenance rehearsal, which keeps it active and may support transfer to LTM.
Retrieval brings the code from LTM into STM so Leah can recall it.
slides.misconceptions: Pupils may confuse the process with the store: attention and rehearsal are processes, while the sensory register, STM and LTM are stores. Repeating the code does not guarantee that it reaches LTM. Model the route: sensory register → attention → STM → rehearsal may support LTM; retrieval returns it to STM.
slides.background: The example applies the model’s processes to a familiar task. The code is heard, so it can be maintained in STM using acoustic rehearsal.
slides.run: Allow about 8 minutes. Pupils write one or two sentences for each stage independently, then compare with a partner. Take answers for each stage and correct store/process terminology.

slides.misconceptions: Pupils may assume that any repetition creates a permanent memory, or that information cannot be forgotten while it is in STM. Explain that brief repetition can keep information active in STM; the model proposes that prolonged rehearsal supports transfer to LTM, but does not guarantee it.
slides.background: This qualification helps avoid an oversimplified account of the model. Later research has questioned whether rehearsal alone explains how information enters LTM.
slides.run: Spend about 5 minutes discussing the difference between keeping information active now and retaining it later. Ask pupils for an example of a number they could repeat briefly but might soon forget.

answers: It is maintained in mainly acoustic STM.
slides.misconceptions: “It is guaranteed to remain in LTM for life” confuses rehearsal with guaranteed transfer and retention. “Repetition retrieves it from LTM every time” confuses rehearsal with retrieval, which brings information from LTM into STM. “It remains in the sensory register throughout” ignores that attention transfers selected information to STM. The best answer is that it is maintained in mainly acoustic STM.
slides.background: Acoustic coding is the typical coding associated with STM in the model. Repeating spoken information is maintenance rehearsal.
slides.run: Allow about 3 minutes for pupils to choose an answer individually, then ask them to justify it to a partner. Check the answer and briefly address why each distractor is wrong.

slides.misconceptions: Pupils may think a filled delay should reduce recall of all list positions equally, or that recency is evidence for LTM. Explain that the filled delay prevents rehearsal and reduces the recency effect, consistent with final items being held in STM; relatively intact primacy is consistent with early items having had more opportunity for rehearsal and LTM storage.
slides.background: In the serial position effect, primacy refers to better recall of early list items and recency to better recall of final items. A filled delay, such as counting backwards, occupies attention and limits rehearsal before recall.
slides.run: Spend about 6 minutes explaining the immediate and delayed recall comparison. Ask pupils to identify what the filled delay is intended to prevent and what change in final-word recall the model predicts.

slides.misconceptions: Pupils may assume that all STM abilities must be impaired together because STM is one store. KF’s verbal STM was severely impaired while visual STM was relatively preserved, which challenges a uniform STM store. This challenges the model’s single STM store but does not by itself show that all of its claims are wrong.
slides.background: KF’s case study is commonly used to support the idea that STM may contain separate components for verbal and visual information. A case study provides detailed evidence about one person, so conclusions should be cautious.
slides.run: Spend about 5 minutes reviewing what KF’s contrasting performance suggests. Ask pupils to state the evidence and then explain how it challenges the idea of one uniform STM store.

slides.misconceptions: Pupils may claim that the serial position findings prove the model, or that the filled delay affects LTM items most. The evidence supports separate stores because recency fell while primacy remained relatively intact, but it does not prove the model. Explain that the delay particularly disrupts rehearsal or maintenance of recent STM items.
slides.background: A claim–evidence–link structure helps pupils connect research findings to a theoretical explanation. Evidence can support a model without ruling out alternative explanations.
slides.run: Spend about 5 minutes unpacking the claim, evidence and link. Ask pupils to identify which phrase gives the evidence and which explains why it supports separate stores.

answers: KF’s case study challenges the idea of one uniform STM store. His verbal STM was severely impaired, especially for heard material, while his visual STM was relatively preserved. This suggests that verbal and visual short-term memory may rely on different components, although one case study cannot establish this for everyone.

With immediate recall, final words should be recalled relatively well because they are still available in STM, and early words should also be recalled relatively well because they may have been rehearsed and transferred to LTM. After counting backwards for 30 seconds, recall of final words should fall because the delay disrupts rehearsal and maintenance in STM. Recall of early words should be less affected because they are more likely to have been transferred to LTM.

The result could support some predictions of the model, but it cannot prove every part. A classroom word-list task tests only a limited situation, and other factors, such as attention or word familiarity, may affect recall.
slides.misconceptions: Pupils may say KF proves there are exactly two STM stores; it challenges a single uniform store but one case cannot establish the full structure. They may predict that counting backwards improves recency or affects early and final words equally. Explain that the task prevents rehearsal, so the model predicts reduced recall of final STM items, while early items may be less affected because of LTM transfer. A supporting result does not prove every part of the model.
slides.background: The counting-backwards task is a filled delay: it reduces rehearsal before recall. The predicted pattern connects the recency effect with STM and the primacy effect with rehearsal and LTM.
slides.run: Allow about 12 minutes. Pupils write the KF claim–evidence–link paragraph and then predict the class result independently. Invite pairs to compare predictions. Finish with the stretch question and take a reason for caution from the class.
